notes: 10 of the 59 entries in data/roster.json. The first five were chosen to exercise every branch of the schema — storage classes none/moderate/high, vitamin/mineral/phytonutrient categories, Tier 2 vs Tier 3, and ULs that are total / supplemental-only / absent entirely.

The five macronutrients (protein, carbohydrate, total fat, fiber, water) were written next because they drive the headline figures on every screen. Total fat has no EAR, RDA or adult AI — only an AMDR — which is why the schema gained an optional `amdr` block and why a macronutrient renders as an acceptable range band rather than a point target.

Energy is deliberately absent from this file. It has no reference intake to look up: an Estimated Energy Requirement is computed per person from a published equation, which lives in lib/nutrition/energy.ts and is labelled an estimate wherever it appears. See docs/DECISIONS.md (D13).
topSources[].fdcId is null throughout. IDs are resolved by the Phase 0 FoodData Central importer — hand-written IDs silently link to the wrong food, which is worse than no link at all.
topSources[].per100g values are approximate, authored from published composition data. The Phase 0 importer overwrites them with exact FDC figures.

Reference intakes are transcribed from the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements Health Professional fact sheets, which restate the IOM/NASEM Dietary Reference Intakes. Verify against the linked citation before shipping.

Infant life-stage groups (0-12 months) are deliberately omitted. This app does not serve that population, and their values are Adequate Intakes derived from breast-milk composition rather than requirements.

nutrients.name: Magnesium
nutrients.oneLiner: Powers muscles and nerves, and helps you wind down at night.
nutrients.simpleExplanation: Your body uses magnesium in hundreds of everyday processes — turning food into energy, letting muscles relax after they contract, and settling your nervous system down for sleep. Roughly half of people don't get quite enough, and the signs are easy to miss: cramps, poor sleep, feeling wired but tired. Seeds, nuts, beans, and leafy greens are the richest sources.
nutrients.summary: Cofactor in over 300 enzymatic reactions, most notably as the counter-ion that stabilizes ATP. Mg-ATP, not free ATP, is the biologically active substrate for essentially all kinases. Also acts as a physiological calcium antagonist at NMDA receptors and in excitation-contraction coupling.
whatItDoes: Stabilizes ATP — the active intracellular form is the Mg-ATP complex
Required cofactor for all kinases, DNA and RNA polymerases, and the ribosome
Antagonizes calcium at NMDA receptors and in smooth and skeletal muscle contraction
Required for the hepatic and renal hydroxylation steps that activate vitamin D
Modulates parathyroid hormone secretion and skeletal calcium handling

benefits.claim: Reduces the frequency of migraine attacks
benefits.note: Several RCTs at 400–600 mg/day show reduced attack frequency; effect sizes are modest and trial quality is mixed. The American Headache Society rates it Level B.

benefits.claim: Modestly lowers blood pressure
benefits.note: Meta-analyses of supplementation trials find reductions on the order of 2 mmHg systolic — real but small, and larger in people who were deficient to begin with.

benefits.claim: Improves subjective sleep quality
benefits.note: Small trials in older adults with insomnia report improvement, but samples are tiny and results have not been replicated at scale. Widely marketed well beyond what the evidence supports.

benefits.claim: Reduces exercise-associated muscle cramps
benefits.note: Mechanistically plausible and popular, but trials in athletes and in pregnancy have been largely null. Cramping has many causes unrelated to magnesium status.

deficiency.prevalence: Around 48% of the US population consumes less than the EAR from food (NHANES). Frank clinical hypomagnesemia is much rarer, because the kidney conserves magnesium efficiently.
riskGroups: type 2 diabetes (urinary losses rise with glycosuria)
chronic alcohol use
long-term proton pump inhibitor use
Crohn's disease, celiac disease, and other malabsorptive conditions
older adults (lower intake plus reduced absorption)
people taking loop or thiazide diuretics

excess.fromFood: Not observed in people with normal kidney function. Excess dietary magnesium is simply excreted, which is why the UL applies to supplements only.
fromSupplements: diarrhea (the classic first sign, and the basis of magnesium's use as a laxative)
nausea
abdominal cramping
excess.severeRisk: At extreme doses: hypotension, respiratory depression, and cardiac arrest. Essentially confined to renal impairment or massive supplemental overdose.

enhancers: adequate vitamin D status
fermentable fiber and inulin (increase colonic absorption)
spreading intake across several meals
inhibitors: phytates in whole grains and legumes
very high supplemental calcium doses
high alcohol intake (increases urinary loss)
excess zinc supplementation
absorption.notes: Fractional absorption falls as intake rises, so several modest doses beat one large one. Soaking, sprouting, or fermenting legumes and grains reduces phytate and improves availability. Magnesium oxide — the cheapest and most common supplemental form — is poorly absorbed; citrate and glycinate are substantially better.

interactions.effect: High-dose calcium supplements reduce magnesium absorption through shared transport. Calcium from food does not meaningfully interfere.
Magnesium is a required cofactor for the enzymes that activate vitamin D. Low magnesium blunts the response to vitamin D supplementation.
Zinc doses above roughly 140 mg/day interfere with magnesium absorption. Dietary amounts are not a concern.

ul.note: Applies only to magnesium from supplements and medications. There is no upper limit for magnesium from food — do not raise an excess alert on dietary intake alone.

citations.label: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Magnesium (Health Professional)

nutrients.name: Vitamin D
nutrients.oneLiner: Lets your body absorb calcium, and behaves more like a hormone than a vitamin.
nutrients.simpleExplanation: Vitamin D controls how much calcium you absorb from food, which makes it essential for bones. Your skin makes it from sunlight, so how much you need from food depends on where you live, your skin tone, and how much time you spend outside. Very few foods contain much of it — oily fish and fortified milk are the main ones — so a lot of people are low in winter. It's stored in body fat for months, which is why a single low day means nothing.
nutrients.summary: A secosteroid prohormone rather than a true vitamin. Cutaneous synthesis from 7-dehydrocholesterol under UVB dominates in most people; dietary intake is secondary. Sequential 25-hydroxylation in the liver and 1α-hydroxylation in the kidney yield calcitriol, which acts through the nuclear vitamin D receptor to regulate several hundred genes. Status is assessed by serum 25(OH)D, not intake.
whatItDoes: Upregulates intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption — the primary and best-established role
Regulates osteoblast and osteoclast activity in bone remodeling
Suppresses parathyroid hormone secretion
Modulates innate and adaptive immune function via VDR expression on immune cells
Influences skeletal muscle function, particularly in older adults

benefits.claim: Prevents rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults
benefits.note: Established physiological necessity. This is what vitamin D is for; the causal relationship is not in question.

benefits.claim: Reduces fracture risk when combined with calcium in older adults
benefits.note: Effect is consistent for combined calcium plus vitamin D in institutionalized and deficient populations. Vitamin D alone in replete community-dwelling adults has been largely null.

benefits.claim: Reduces the risk of acute respiratory infection
benefits.note: A 2017 individual-participant meta-analysis found a small protective effect concentrated in people who were deficient at baseline. Subsequent large trials have been inconsistent.

benefits.claim: Prevents cancer or cardiovascular disease
benefits.note: Strong observational associations were not borne out. VITAL — 25,871 participants, 2,000 IU/day, 5.3 years — found no reduction in cancer incidence or major cardiovascular events. Treat as unsupported for primary prevention.

deficiency.clinicalName: vitamin D deficiency (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults)
deficiency.prevalence: Roughly 18% of the US population has serum 25(OH)D below 40 nmol/L (at risk of inadequacy), with markedly higher rates in people with darker skin, at higher latitudes, and in winter.
earlySigns: bone aching, especially in the lower back and hips
advancedSigns: rickets in children: bowed legs, delayed growth, skeletal deformity
riskGroups: people with darker skin (melanin reduces cutaneous synthesis)
residents above roughly 37° latitude in winter
people with limited sun exposure — housebound, veiled, night-shift workers
older adults (skin synthesis declines markedly with age)
obesity (sequestration in adipose tissue lowers circulating levels)
fat malabsorption: celiac, Crohn's, cystic fibrosis, post-bariatric surgery
exclusively breastfed infants without supplementation

excess.fromFood: Not achievable from unfortified food. Reported toxicity is essentially always from supplements or from manufacturing errors in fortified products.
fromSupplements: hypercalcemia
nausea and vomiting
excessive thirst and urination
confusion
kidney stones
excess.severeRisk: Sustained hypercalcemia causes vascular and soft-tissue calcification and renal failure. Typically requires prolonged intake well above 10,000 IU/day; sunlight alone cannot cause it, because excess previtamin D is photodegraded in the skin.

absorption.typicalRate: ~50% of dietary intake; cutaneous synthesis is the dominant source for most people
enhancers: consumption with a fat-containing meal
adequate magnesium status (required for the activating hydroxylases)
UVB exposure to skin — the main source, not food
inhibitors: fat malabsorption of any cause
obesity (sequestration in adipose tissue)
sunscreen, clothing, glass, and darker skin pigmentation (all reduce synthesis)
corticosteroids and some anticonvulsants (accelerate catabolism)
absorption.notes: Because storage is measured in months, day-to-day intake is a poor guide to status — serum 25(OH)D is the meaningful measure. D3 (cholecalciferol) raises and maintains serum levels more effectively than D2 (ergocalciferol). Latitude and season dominate: above roughly 37°N, cutaneous synthesis is negligible from November to February regardless of time spent outdoors.

interactions.effect: The hepatic and renal hydroxylases that activate vitamin D are magnesium-dependent. Correcting low magnesium can improve vitamin D status without any change in vitamin D intake.
Vitamin D's principal function is enabling calcium absorption. Fracture-prevention benefit is seen for the pair, not for vitamin D alone.
Vitamin K-dependent proteins direct the calcium that vitamin D makes available toward bone rather than vasculature. Clinically suggestive; not yet established.

ul.note: 100 mcg equals 4,000 IU. Sunlight cannot push intake past this — excess previtamin D3 is photodegraded in the skin — so the UL is effectively a limit on supplements and fortified foods.

citations.label: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Vitamin D (Health Professional)
VITAL trial — Vitamin D supplements and prevention of cancer and cardiovascular disease (NEJM 2019)

nutrients.name: Vitamin B12
nutrients.oneLiner: Builds red blood cells and protects your nerves. Only found in animal foods.
nutrients.simpleExplanation: B12 is needed to make red blood cells and to maintain the insulating sheath around your nerves. It occurs naturally only in animal foods, so anyone eating plant-based needs fortified foods or a supplement — this is not optional. Your liver stores several years' worth, which is why deficiency takes a long time to appear and why one low day means nothing. The catch is that nerve damage from prolonged deficiency can be permanent, so it's worth not finding out the slow way.
nutrients.summary: A cobalt-containing corrinoid, the largest and most structurally complex vitamin. Functions as a cofactor for exactly two mammalian enzymes: methionine synthase (cytosolic, remethylating homocysteine to methionine) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (mitochondrial, in odd-chain fatty acid and branched-chain amino acid catabolism). Absorption requires gastric intrinsic factor and an intact terminal ileum, making it uniquely vulnerable to gastrointestinal pathology.
whatItDoes: Cofactor for methionine synthase — regenerates methionine and releases folate from the 5-methyl-THF trap
Cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in propionate metabolism
Required for myelin synthesis and maintenance
Required for DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells, notably erythroid precursors

benefits.claim: Prevents megaloblastic anemia
benefits.note: Established physiological necessity. Deficiency causes it; repletion resolves it.

benefits.claim: Prevents irreversible peripheral and central neuropathy
benefits.note: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord is a well-characterized consequence of prolonged deficiency. Early repletion reverses it; late repletion does not.

benefits.claim: Lowers plasma homocysteine
benefits.note: The biochemical effect is reliable and dose-dependent. Whether lowering homocysteine improves clinical outcomes is a separate question — see below.

benefits.claim: Reduces cardiovascular events or slows cognitive decline
benefits.note: Despite reliable homocysteine lowering, large RCTs (HOPE-2, SEARCH, VITATOPS) have not shown reductions in cardiovascular events. Cognitive trials in people who are B12-replete have likewise been null. Benefit appears confined to correcting actual deficiency.

deficiency.clinicalName: vitamin B12 deficiency; pernicious anemia when caused by loss of intrinsic factor
deficiency.prevalence: Approximately 6% of adults under 60 and closer to 20% of adults over 60 in the US and UK, driven mainly by absorptive failure rather than low intake. Rates among people eating strictly plant-based without supplementation are far higher.
earlySigns: pins and needles in hands and feet
advancedSigns: subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
riskGroups: people eating vegan or strict vegetarian diets without supplementation
adults over 60 (atrophic gastritis reduces the acid needed to free B12 from food protein)
long-term metformin use
long-term proton pump inhibitor or H2 blocker use
pernicious anemia (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor)
post-gastrectomy or ileal resection
Crohn's disease affecting the terminal ileum

excess.fromFood: No adverse effects have been associated with excess B12 intake from food or supplements in healthy people.
fromSupplements: no established toxicity
acneiform eruptions and rosacea flares reported at very high supplemental doses, uncommonly

absorption.typicalRate: ~50% of a small dose; falls sharply as dose rises because intrinsic-factor-mediated uptake saturates near 1.5–2 mcg per meal
enhancers: adequate gastric acid (frees B12 from food protein)
intact intrinsic factor production
splitting intake across meals rather than one large dose
crystalline B12 in fortified foods and supplements — does not require gastric acid to be released
inhibitors: atrophic gastritis and reduced gastric acid
proton pump inhibitors and H2 blockers
metformin (interferes with ileal uptake)
loss of intrinsic factor (pernicious anemia)
terminal ileal disease or resection
heavy alcohol use
absorption.notes: The receptor-mediated pathway saturates at roughly 1.5–2 mcg per meal, so total daily absorption is bounded by meal frequency rather than dose size. A separate passive diffusion route absorbs about 1% of any dose regardless of intrinsic factor — which is why high-dose oral supplementation (1,000 mcg) works even in pernicious anemia, where the active pathway is absent entirely.

interactions.effect: The two are tightly coupled through methionine synthase. Critically, high folate intake can correct B12-deficiency anemia on a blood count while neurological damage continues to progress unnoticed — the reason folic acid fortification levels are capped.
Large vitamin C doses taken with a meal may degrade B12 in vitro. Clinical relevance is doubtful; separating them by a couple of hours resolves any concern.

citations.label: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Vitamin B12 (Health Professional)

nutrients.name: Vitamin C
nutrients.oneLiner: Builds collagen, and dramatically boosts iron absorption from plant foods.
nutrients.simpleExplanation: Vitamin C is what your body uses to build collagen — the protein holding skin, blood vessels, and gums together — and it makes iron from plant foods far easier to absorb. Your body doesn't store it, so you need some most days. The good news is it's easy to get: one red pepper or one kiwi covers a full day. It does not prevent colds, despite the reputation, though it does shorten them slightly.
nutrients.summary: A water-soluble reducing agent and essential cofactor for a family of copper- and iron-containing enzymes. Humans, other primates, and guinea pigs cannot synthesize it due to loss of L-gulonolactone oxidase. Serves as the electron donor for the prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases that stabilize the collagen triple helix, and for dopamine β-hydroxylase in catecholamine synthesis. Plasma levels are tightly controlled by renal reabsorption, which saturates near 400 mg/day intake.
whatItDoes: Cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase in collagen cross-linking
Reduces dietary non-heme iron from Fe3+ to the absorbable Fe2+ form
Cofactor for dopamine β-hydroxylase in noradrenaline synthesis
Cofactor for carnitine biosynthesis
Regenerates oxidized vitamin E back to its active form
Scavenges aqueous-phase reactive oxygen species

benefits.claim: Prevents scurvy
benefits.note: Established physiological necessity. Roughly 10 mg/day prevents it — far below the RDA, which targets tissue saturation rather than bare adequacy.

benefits.claim: Substantially increases non-heme iron absorption
benefits.note: Consistent and large: 50 mg of vitamin C taken alongside a plant-based iron source can multiply absorption several-fold. One of the most practically useful nutrient interactions there is.

benefits.claim: Shortens the duration of the common cold
benefits.note: Cochrane review of regular supplementation: about 8% shorter in adults, 14% in children. Real, consistent, and small — roughly half a day.

benefits.claim: Prevents the common cold
benefits.note: Explicitly NOT supported in the general population — the same Cochrane review found no reduction in incidence. The one exception is people under extreme physical stress (marathon runners, soldiers in subarctic conditions), where incidence roughly halved. Worth stating plainly given how widely the opposite is believed.

deficiency.prevalence: Roughly 7% of the US population has serum levels indicating deficiency (NHANES), concentrated among smokers and people with low fruit and vegetable intake. Frank scurvy is rare but persistently under-diagnosed in people with restrictive diets, alcohol dependence, or severe mental illness.
advancedSigns: bleeding, swollen gums and loosening teeth
poor wound healing and reopening of old scars
riskGroups: smokers (need an additional 35 mg/day due to oxidative turnover)
people with very limited dietary variety
alcohol dependence
people on dialysis
severe malabsorptive conditions
infants fed exclusively on boiled or evaporated milk

excess.fromFood: No adverse effects from food sources. Renal excretion handles any dietary excess.
fromSupplements: diarrhea and abdominal cramping
nausea
increased urinary oxalate, relevant to kidney stone formers
false readings on some blood glucose meters
excess.severeRisk: Doses above roughly 1,000 mg/day may raise oxalate stone risk in susceptible people. In hereditary hemochromatosis, high doses can worsen iron overload by increasing absorption.

absorption.typicalRate: 70–90% at typical intakes; falls below 50% above 1,000 mg in a single dose
enhancers: splitting intake across the day
consuming from whole foods, where it arrives with flavonoids
inhibitors: smoking (increases metabolic turnover rather than blocking absorption)
heat — vitamin C is among the most cooking-labile nutrients
prolonged storage and exposure to air
boiling, which leaches it into the water
absorption.notes: Active transport saturates, so absorption efficiency falls steeply with dose — 200 mg taken twice beats 400 mg taken once. Cooking losses are substantial: boiling can destroy over half the vitamin C in a vegetable, while steaming, microwaving, and raw consumption preserve much more. Storage matters too; a cut pepper loses vitamin C over days in the fridge.

interactions.effect: Reduces Fe3+ to absorbable Fe2+ and forms a soluble chelate. The single most effective dietary lever for improving iron status on a plant-based diet.
Regenerates the oxidized tocopheroxyl radical back to active vitamin E, letting each vitamin E molecule work repeatedly.
Very high supplemental doses may impair copper status. Not a concern at dietary intakes.

ul.note: Smokers require an additional 35 mg/day above the RDA. The UL is set by gastrointestinal tolerance, not systemic toxicity.

citations.label: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Vitamin C (Health Professional)
Cochrane Review — Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold

nutrients.name: Lutein + Zeaxanthin
nutrients.oneLiner: Yellow pigments that concentrate in the retina and filter blue light.
nutrients.simpleExplanation: These two pigments come from leafy greens, egg yolks, and corn, and your body sends them straight to the centre of the retina, where they form a yellow filter that absorbs blue light. Eating more of them measurably thickens that filter. There's no official daily requirement — nobody gets a deficiency disease from lacking them — but higher intakes are linked to slower age-related macular degeneration.
nutrients.summary: Xanthophyll carotenoids, and the only two dietary carotenoids selectively accumulated in the primate macula, where they constitute macular pigment. Zeaxanthin dominates the foveal center, lutein the periphery. Both absorb strongly in the blue region (~450 nm) and quench singlet oxygen. Macular pigment optical density responds measurably to dietary and supplemental intake, making this one of the few phytonutrients with a validated tissue-level biomarker.
whatItDoes: Forms macular pigment, filtering blue light before it reaches photoreceptors
Quenches singlet oxygen and peroxyl radicals in the retina, a uniquely high-oxidative-stress tissue
Reduces chromatic aberration and light scatter, improving contrast sensitivity
Accumulates in brain tissue, where concentrations correlate with cognitive measures

benefits.claim: Slows progression of age-related macular degeneration in people who already have it
benefits.note: AREDS2 (n=4,203) found lutein + zeaxanthin an effective and safer replacement for beta-carotene in the AREDS formulation. Benefit was clearest in participants with the lowest baseline dietary intake. This is progression in existing AMD, not prevention in healthy eyes.

benefits.claim: Increases macular pigment optical density
benefits.note: A reliable, dose-dependent biomarker response, consistently reproduced. Note this is a tissue measurement, not a clinical outcome — pigment density rising is not the same as vision improving.

benefits.claim: Improves contrast sensitivity and glare recovery
benefits.note: Several small trials in healthy adults report improvement; samples are small and outcome measures vary between studies.

benefits.claim: Supports cognitive function in older adults
benefits.note: Observational associations between macular pigment density and cognitive scores, plus small pilot trials. Mechanistically interesting, not established.

deficiency.prevalence: Not applicable — there is no deficiency state. US median intake is roughly 1–2 mg/day, well below the 10 mg used in intervention trials.
riskGroups: people with very low vegetable intake (low macular pigment density is a risk marker, not a deficiency)
smokers (lower circulating carotenoid levels overall)

excess.fromFood: No toxicity reported from food. Extremely high intakes of yellow-orange vegetables can produce carotenodermia — harmless yellowing of the skin that resolves on reduction.
fromSupplements: carotenodermia at very high sustained doses
no established toxicity at doses used in trials (up to 20 mg/day)

absorption.typicalRate: Highly variable, roughly 5–60% depending on the food matrix
enhancers: dietary fat consumed in the same meal — these are fat-soluble and absorption is poor without it
cooking and chopping (disrupts plant cell walls)
egg yolk matrix, which is unusually bioavailable despite modest absolute content
inhibitors: very low-fat meals
intact raw plant cell walls
high doses of beta-carotene, which competes for the same absorption pathway
plant sterol supplements and fat-blocking medications
absorption.notes: Food matrix matters more than absolute content here. Egg yolk delivers only about 1 mg per 100 g against spinach's 11 mg, but its lipid matrix makes it far more bioavailable — a fair comparison has to weight for that. Adding oil to a salad is not optional for carotenoid absorption; a fat-free dressing substantially reduces uptake.

interactions.effect: Shares intestinal absorption pathways. High-dose beta-carotene supplementation lowers serum lutein — one of the findings that motivated the AREDS2 substitution.
Both are lipid-phase antioxidants concentrated in retinal membranes and appear to act complementarily.

populationMedian.source: NHANES, US adults — combined lutein and zeaxanthin

studiedRange.note: AREDS2 used 10 mg lutein plus 2 mg zeaxanthin daily. Observational studies associating higher intake with lower AMD risk generally compare quintiles around 6 mg/day and above.

intakeContext.framing: No official requirement exists for lutein or zeaxanthin, and no deficiency disease has ever been described. These figures show what people typically eat and what amounts have been studied — they are context, not a target to hit.

citations.label: AREDS2 — Lutein + zeaxanthin and omega-3 fatty acids for age-related macular degeneration (JAMA 2013)

nutrients.name: Protein
nutrients.oneLiner: Supplies the amino acids your body cannot make for itself.
nutrients.simpleExplanation: Protein is broken down into amino acids and rebuilt into muscle, enzymes, antibodies and hormones. Nine of those amino acids can't be made by the body at all, so they have to come from food. The official minimum is lower than most people expect — around 56 g a day for an adult man — but that figure is the amount needed to avoid losing tissue, not the amount that is best for building or keeping muscle. Spreading intake across meals works better than eating most of it at dinner.
nutrients.summary: Nitrogen source and the sole dietary supply of the nine indispensable amino acids. The RDA of 0.8 g/kg/day derives from nitrogen-balance studies and represents the intake at which most adults avoid net protein loss — an avoidance-of-deficiency figure, not an optimum. Muscle protein synthesis is stimulated in a saturable, per-meal manner with leucine as the principal trigger, which is why distribution across meals matters independently of total intake.
whatItDoes: Supplies the nine indispensable amino acids, which cannot be synthesised endogenously
Provides the substrate for muscle, connective tissue, enzymes, transport proteins and immunoglobulins
Contributes to satiety more per calorie than carbohydrate or fat
Serves as a gluconeogenic substrate when carbohydrate intake is low
Carries the highest thermic effect of the three macronutrients, at roughly 20–30% of its energy

benefits.claim: Preserves lean mass during weight loss
benefits.note: Consistently reproduced across randomised trials. Higher protein intake during an energy deficit reduces the share of weight lost as lean tissue, with the effect largest when combined with resistance training.

benefits.claim: Increases muscle mass and strength gains from resistance training
benefits.note: Meta-analyses find added benefit up to roughly 1.6 g/kg/day, with a plateau beyond that. Trials above 2.2 g/kg have not shown further gain.

benefits.claim: Improves satiety and reduces spontaneous energy intake
benefits.note: Reliable within single meals and short trials; the effect on long-term body weight is smaller and more variable than short-term appetite data suggest.

benefits.claim: Slows age-related muscle loss in older adults
benefits.note: Older adults show anabolic resistance and appear to need more protein per meal to trigger the same synthetic response. Observational and short-trial support is good; long-term outcome trials are limited.

benefits.claim: High intake damages healthy kidneys
benefits.note: A negative finding, included because the claim is widespread. Trials in people with normal kidney function show no decline in glomerular filtration at intakes up to 2.8 g/kg/day. The concern is real and important in existing chronic kidney disease, and does not generalise to healthy kidneys.

deficiency.prevalence: Rare in high-income countries at the level of frank deficiency. Marginal intake is common in older adults, in people eating very low energy diets, and in some hospitalised populations.
earlySigns: loss of muscle mass and strength
riskGroups: older adults, who need more per meal to trigger the same response
people in a sustained energy deficit
people recovering from surgery, burns or serious illness
poorly planned vegan diets with little legume or soy intake
people with malabsorptive conditions

excess.fromFood: No upper limit has been set. Intakes well above the RDA are not associated with harm in people with normal kidney and liver function, though very high intakes displace other foods and can crowd out fibre and phytonutrients.
fromSupplements: gastrointestinal discomfort from large single doses
displacement of other foods, reducing dietary variety
meaningful risk only where kidney or liver function is already impaired
excess.severeRisk: In existing chronic kidney disease, high protein intake accelerates decline in glomerular filtration and intake should be set with a clinician. There is no equivalent risk in healthy kidneys.

absorption.typicalRate: Over 90% of protein from animal sources; roughly 70–90% from plant sources
enhancers: cooking, which denatures protein and improves digestibility
combining plant sources across the day to cover all indispensable amino acids
spreading intake across three or four meals rather than one large one
resistance exercise, which raises the synthetic response to a given dose
inhibitors: trypsin inhibitors in raw legumes
tannins and phytates in some whole plant foods
very large single doses, where the per-meal synthetic response saturates
advanced age, through anabolic resistance
absorption.notes: Digestibility and amino acid pattern both matter, which is why DIAAS is a better guide than raw grams for plant-based diets. Lysine is the limiting amino acid in cereals and methionine in legumes, so the two complement each other — but they do not need to be eaten in the same meal, only across the day. Leucine is the principal trigger for muscle protein synthesis, and a threshold of roughly 2.5 g of leucine per meal is where the response reliably saturates in younger adults.

interactions.effect: Higher protein intake raises urinary calcium but also increases intestinal calcium absorption. Net effect on bone is neutral to positive when calcium intake is adequate — the old 'protein leaches calcium from bone' claim does not hold at normal intakes.
Meat, fish and poultry contain a factor that substantially improves absorption of non-heme iron eaten in the same meal, on top of supplying heme iron directly.
B6 is the cofactor for transamination and other amino acid metabolism, so B6 requirement rises with protein intake.

amdr.note: Percent of total energy. The lower bound is close to the RDA for most adults; the upper bound is where the evidence for safety and adequacy stops, not a point at which harm begins.

citations.label: NASEM — Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids
Morton et al. — Systematic review and meta-analysis of protein supplementation on resistance-training gains (BJSM 2018)

nutrients.name: Total carbohydrate
nutrients.oneLiner: The body's most readily used fuel, and the brain's preferred one.
nutrients.simpleExplanation: Carbohydrate is the fuel your body reaches for first, and the brain runs on glucose almost exclusively. The 130 g daily figure is the amount that covers the brain without the body having to make glucose from protein or fat — it is a floor, not a goal, and most people eat well above it. What matters far more than the total is the form: the same 40 g behaves very differently coming from lentils than from a soft drink.
nutrients.summary: Primary oxidative substrate and the only fuel the brain uses in appreciable quantity under normal feeding. The 130 g/day RDA is derived from mean cerebral glucose utilisation and represents the intake below which gluconeogenesis from amino acids and glycerol must supply the deficit — a physiological floor, not an optimum. Glycemic response depends on food matrix, fibre content, processing and co-ingested fat and protein far more than on total grams, which is why glycemic load is tracked per meal rather than inferred from carbohydrate mass.
whatItDoes: Supplies glucose, effectively the sole fuel of the brain under normal feeding conditions
Replenishes muscle and liver glycogen, which determines capacity for high-intensity work
Spares protein from being catabolised for gluconeogenesis
Provides the fermentable substrate that feeds colonic bacteria, via its fibre and resistant starch fractions
Determines the postprandial glucose and insulin response, in a form-dependent way

benefits.claim: Adequate intake supports high-intensity and endurance exercise performance
benefits.note: Among the best-replicated findings in sports nutrition. Glycogen availability is limiting for sustained work above roughly 70% of VO2max.

benefits.claim: Lower-glycemic-load diets improve glycemic control in type 2 diabetes
benefits.note: Meta-analyses find modest but consistent reductions in HbA1c, on the order of 0.3–0.5 percentage points. Real, and smaller than commonly claimed.

benefits.claim: Lower-glycemic-load diets reduce acne severity
benefits.note: A small number of randomised trials show improvement, supported by consistent observational data. Associated, not established — the trials are small and hard to blind.

benefits.claim: Carbohydrate restriction is superior for long-term weight loss
benefits.note: A negative finding worth stating plainly. Head-to-head trials of low-carbohydrate against low-fat diets matched for energy and protein find little difference beyond twelve months. Adherence predicts the outcome, not macronutrient ratio.

deficiency.prevalence: There is no deficiency disease. Sustained intake below roughly 50 g/day induces nutritional ketosis, which is an adaptation rather than a pathology.
earlySigns: fatigue and reduced capacity for high-intensity exercise
headache and difficulty concentrating during adaptation
constipation, where fibre falls with the carbohydrate
advancedSigns: loss of lean mass where protein intake is not raised to compensate
menstrual disturbance at very low intakes combined with an energy deficit
riskGroups: athletes in high-volume training on restricted intakes
people on very-low-carbohydrate diets without clinical supervision
people with type 1 diabetes, where carbohydrate intake and insulin must be matched

excess.fromFood: No upper limit has been set for total carbohydrate. The DRI committee did set a limit on added sugars — under 25% of total energy — on the grounds that above that they displace nutrient-dense foods, and most public health bodies since have recommended considerably less.
fromSupplements: gastrointestinal distress from concentrated sports carbohydrate above roughly 60–90 g/hour
dental caries from frequent free-sugar exposure
displacement of nutrient-dense foods where intake comes largely from refined sources

absorption.typicalRate: Near-complete for digestible carbohydrate; fibre and resistant starch pass to the colon undigested
enhancers: cooking and processing, which gelatinise starch and speed digestion
finer particle size, as in flour against intact grain
inhibitors: intact cell walls in whole grains and legumes
viscous soluble fibre, which slows gastric emptying
fat and protein eaten in the same meal
acidity, including vinegar and sourdough fermentation
cooling of cooked starch, which forms resistant starch
absorption.notes: The same grams of carbohydrate produce very different glucose curves depending on form. Whole intact grains produce a markedly lower response than flour made from the same grain, and legumes lower still. This is why the app tracks glycemic load per meal — computed from the food's own glycemic index and its available carbohydrate — rather than inferring anything from total carbohydrate alone.

interactions.effect: Fibre is a carbohydrate fraction that is not digested, and it substantially blunts the glucose response of the digestible fraction eaten alongside it. Available carbohydrate — total minus fibre — is what drives glycemic load.

Thiamin is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, so the requirement scales with carbohydrate oxidation. Diets high in refined carbohydrate supply the demand without the thiamin that whole grains would have carried.
Chromium contributes to insulin signalling, and high intakes of refined carbohydrate increase its urinary loss.

amdr.note: Percent of total energy. Well-conducted diets sit outside this band in both directions without evident harm; the band reflects the range the DRI committee could support, not a boundary of safety.

citations.label: NASEM — Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids
Atkinson, Brand-Miller et al. — International Tables of Glycemic Index and Glycemic Load Values 2021

nutrients.name: Total fat
nutrients.oneLiner: Carries the fat-soluble vitamins and supplies the two fats you must eat.
nutrients.simpleExplanation: Fat is the densest source of energy, and it is also the vehicle: vitamins A, D, E and K and the carotenoids are barely absorbed without it. Two fatty acids — linoleic and alpha-linolenic — cannot be made by the body at all. There is no recommended daily amount for fat as a whole, only a sensible range of 20–35% of your calories, because which fats you eat matters far more than how much.
nutrients.summary: Energy-dense substrate at 9 kcal/g, structural component of every cell membrane, and the obligatory carrier for fat-soluble micronutrients and carotenoids. Total fat carries no EAR, RDA or adult AI — only an AMDR of 20–35% of energy — because outcome data track fatty acid composition rather than total quantity. The two indispensable fatty acids, linoleic (n-6) and alpha-linolenic (n-3), each carry their own AI and are tracked separately in this app.
whatItDoes: Supplies linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid, the two fatty acids humans cannot synthesise
Enables absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K and of the carotenoids
Forms the phospholipid bilayer of every cell membrane, with composition affecting membrane fluidity
Provides the substrate for eicosanoid and steroid hormone synthesis
Slows gastric emptying, blunting the glycemic response of a meal

benefits.claim: Replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated fat lowers cardiovascular risk
benefits.note: Among the most robust findings in nutrition, supported by randomised controlled trials, prospective cohorts and a clear mechanism. Note the finding is about substitution — replacing saturated fat with refined carbohydrate shows no benefit.

benefits.claim: Dietary fat is required for absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and carotenoids
benefits.note: Established physiology. A fat-free dressing measurably reduces carotenoid uptake from the same salad.

benefits.claim: Mediterranean-pattern diets high in monounsaturated fat reduce cardiovascular events
benefits.note: PREDIMED found a reduction in major cardiovascular events with added olive oil or nuts. The trial was retracted and republished after randomisation irregularities were found at some sites; the reanalysis reached similar conclusions, but with the effect estimated less precisely than the original headline.

benefits.claim: Dietary cholesterol meaningfully raises blood cholesterol in most people
benefits.note: A negative finding, kept because the belief persists. The response varies substantially between individuals and is small on average; the 300 mg/day limit was dropped from the US Dietary Guidelines in 2015. Saturated and trans fat intake matter considerably more.

deficiency.prevalence: Very rare from ordinary diets. Seen historically in patients on fat-free parenteral nutrition and in severe fat malabsorption.
advancedSigns: clinical signs of vitamin A, D, E or K deficiency
riskGroups: people with cystic fibrosis, pancreatic insufficiency or cholestatic liver disease
people after bariatric surgery
people on very-low-fat diets sustained over long periods
patients on long-term fat-free parenteral nutrition

excess.fromFood: No upper limit has been set for total fat. Limits exist for the components that carry the risk: saturated fat under 10% of energy in most guidelines, and trans fat as low as achievable.
fromSupplements: gastrointestinal discomfort and loose stools from large doses of oils
displacement of other foods, given the energy density
excess.severeRisk: Industrially produced trans fat raises LDL and lowers HDL simultaneously and has no safe intake. It is a component of total fat and is tracked separately in this app.

absorption.typicalRate: Around 95% of dietary fat in healthy adults
enhancers: bile acid secretion, triggered by fat entering the duodenum
pancreatic lipase and colipase
emulsification through cooking or blending
medium-chain triglycerides, which bypass the usual micellar route
inhibitors: pancreatic insufficiency or cholestasis
orlistat and other lipase inhibitors
plant sterol supplements at high doses
very high fibre intakes, marginally
absorption.notes: Fat absorption is efficient enough that the interesting question is composition, not quantity. Because fat is the carrier for carotenoids and the fat-soluble vitamins, a meal's fat content changes how much micronutrient you actually get from it — which is why a fat-free dressing on a salad is a false economy.

interactions.effect: Fat-soluble. Absorption is substantially reduced when taken with a low-fat meal, which matters for both dietary and supplemental vitamin D.
Absorbed through the same micellar pathway. Vitamin E requirement also rises with polyunsaturated fat intake, since it protects those fatty acids from peroxidation.
Fat-soluble; uptake from leafy greens is markedly better when the meal contains fat.
Carotenoid absorption is poor to negligible without fat in the same meal. A few grams of oil is enough to change the outcome substantially.

amdr.note: Percent of total energy. Total fat has no RDA and no adult AI — this band is the only reference intake published for it, because health outcomes track which fats you eat rather than how much fat in total.

citations.label: NASEM — Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids
Cochrane Review — Reduction in saturated fat intake for cardiovascular disease

nutrients.name: Fiber, total
nutrients.oneLiner: Feeds your gut bacteria and is the single most under-eaten thing in the diet.
nutrients.simpleExplanation: Fibre is the part of plant food you don't digest, so it reaches the colon intact and feeds the bacteria living there. Roughly 95% of people fall short of the recommended amount, which makes it the largest gap in most diets. You cannot get a deficiency disease from lacking it — which is exactly why it gets ignored — but intake tracks strongly with lower rates of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and bowel cancer. Increase it gradually and drink more water, or the first week will be uncomfortable.
nutrients.summary: Non-digestible carbohydrate polymers reaching the colon intact. Soluble, viscous and fermentable fractions lower LDL and blunt glycemic response; insoluble fractions increase stool bulk and reduce transit time. Colonic fermentation yields short-chain fatty acids, principally butyrate, which is the preferred fuel of the colonocyte and a mediator of much of fibre's systemic effect. The AI of 14 g per 1000 kcal derives from the intake associated with the lowest coronary heart disease risk in observational cohorts — a risk-reduction figure, not a requirement, since no deficiency state exists.
whatItDoes: Supplies fermentable substrate to the colonic microbiota, producing butyrate, propionate and acetate
Increases stool bulk and reduces transit time via its insoluble fraction
Binds bile acids, forcing hepatic cholesterol into replacement synthesis and lowering LDL
Slows gastric emptying and glucose absorption through viscosity
Increases satiety per calorie, both mechanically and hormonally

benefits.claim: Reduces cardiovascular disease risk
benefits.note: A dose-response meta-analysis commissioned by the WHO across 185 prospective studies and 58 trials found a 15–30% reduction in cardiovascular mortality comparing highest to lowest intakes, with benefit continuing up to at least 25–29 g/day.

benefits.claim: Lowers LDL cholesterol
benefits.note: Consistent randomised trial evidence for viscous soluble fibres specifically — oat beta-glucan, psyllium, pectin. Around 3 g/day of beta-glucan lowers LDL by roughly 5–7%.

benefits.claim: Reduces risk of colorectal cancer
benefits.note: Graded 'probable' by the World Cancer Research Fund. Consistent across cohorts, with a plausible butyrate mechanism; randomised trials of fibre supplements on adenoma recurrence have been null, which is why this is not rated strong.

benefits.claim: Improves glycemic control and reduces type 2 diabetes incidence
benefits.note: Strong and consistent cohort data; trial effects on HbA1c are real but modest. Cereal fibre shows the association more clearly than fruit fibre.

benefits.claim: Relieves symptoms in irritable bowel syndrome
benefits.note: Depends entirely on the type. Soluble fibre such as psyllium helps some people; insoluble wheat bran commonly makes IBS symptoms worse. A blanket recommendation to eat more fibre is poor advice here.

deficiency.prevalence: Around 95% of US adults consume less than the Adequate Intake (NHANES). There is no deficiency disease, which is a large part of why the shortfall persists.
advancedSigns: reduced microbial diversity in the colon
riskGroups: people eating mostly refined grains and few vegetables
people on low-carbohydrate diets that were not planned around fibre
people following a strict low-FODMAP diet beyond the elimination phase
older adults with low food intake overall

excess.fromFood: No upper limit has been set. Very high intakes reached suddenly cause bloating, wind and cramping, and can reduce absorption of minerals — but this is a ramp-rate problem far more than a ceiling problem.
fromSupplements: bloating, wind and abdominal cramping, especially when intake rises quickly
reduced absorption of iron, zinc and calcium at very high intakes
oesophageal or intestinal obstruction from bulking agents taken with too little water
excess.severeRisk: Bulk-forming supplements taken without adequate fluid can cause obstruction. This is the one genuine acute risk and it is entirely avoidable.

absorption.typicalRate: Not absorbed by design — fermented in the colon, yielding roughly 2 kcal/g from short-chain fatty acids
enhancers: adequate fluid intake, without which the bulking effect backfires
increasing intake gradually over two to four weeks
variety across fibre types, since different fractions feed different bacteria
resistant starch formed by cooking and then cooling starchy foods
inhibitors: raising intake abruptly, which produces symptoms that lead people to stop
low fluid intake
antibiotic use, which disrupts the fermenting community
absorption.notes: Fibre is not one substance and the fractions do different jobs, which is why this app tracks soluble and insoluble separately where the data exists. Oat beta-glucan and psyllium lower LDL; wheat bran does not, but moves the bowel far more effectively. Getting fibre from a range of whole plant foods rather than one supplement is what the cohort evidence actually describes.

interactions.effect: Fermentable fibre and inulin increase colonic magnesium absorption, partly offsetting the phytate that usually accompanies high-fibre foods.
Phytate in high-fibre plant foods binds non-heme iron and reduces its absorption. Soaking, sprouting and fermenting reduce phytate substantially.
Same phytate mechanism as iron. Relevant at habitually high fibre intakes with marginal zinc, not at ordinary intakes.
Bulking fibre draws water into the stool. Increasing fibre without increasing fluid makes constipation worse rather than better.

citations.label: NASEM — Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids
Reynolds et al. — Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses (The Lancet 2019)

nutrients.name: Water
nutrients.oneLiner: The one nutrient you cannot go more than a few days without.
nutrients.simpleExplanation: Water makes up roughly 60% of your body and is the medium every biochemical reaction happens in. The commonly quoted target of about 3.7 L a day for men and 2.7 L for women is total water — around a fifth of it comes from food, so the amount you actually need to drink is meaningfully lower. There is no need to count it precisely: thirst is a reliable guide for healthy adults, and pale yellow urine is a better check than any number.
nutrients.summary: Solvent and transport medium constituting roughly 60% of body mass in adult men and 50–55% in adult women. Balance is regulated by arginine vasopressin acting on renal collecting-duct aquaporins, with plasma osmolality held within about 1–2% of setpoint. The AI is set from median total water intake in healthy populations rather than from a measured requirement, because requirement varies enormously with climate, activity and diet — a point the DRI committee stated explicitly.
whatItDoes: Acts as the solvent for essentially all metabolic reactions
Transports nutrients, oxygen and metabolic waste through blood and lymph
Regulates core temperature through sweat evaporation
Provides hydrostatic pressure for glomerular filtration and lubricates joints and serous surfaces
Maintains plasma volume, and so cardiovascular function during exertion

benefits.claim: Prevents dehydration and maintains cardiovascular and thermoregulatory function
benefits.note: Established physiology. Performance and cognition both decline measurably at fluid deficits of roughly 2% of body mass.

benefits.claim: Reduces recurrence of kidney stones
benefits.note: Randomised trial evidence: raising urine output above 2 L/day roughly halves recurrence in people who have already formed a stone.

benefits.claim: Aids weight loss when drunk before meals
benefits.note: A handful of small trials show a modest effect, mostly in older adults where gastric emptying is slower. Frequently overstated.

benefits.claim: Everyone needs eight glasses of water a day
benefits.note: A negative finding worth stating, because the figure is everywhere. It has no identifiable scientific origin, ignores the roughly 20% of intake that comes from food, and ignores that requirement varies with body size, climate and activity. Thirst regulates intake adequately in healthy adults.

deficiency.prevalence: Common and usually mild. Clinically meaningful dehydration is frequent in older adults, in whom the thirst response is blunted.
earlySigns: dark yellow urine and reduced output
advancedSigns: acute kidney injury in severe cases
riskGroups: older adults, whose thirst response declines with age
endurance athletes and outdoor workers in heat
people with vomiting, diarrhoea or fever
people on diuretics
people with poorly controlled diabetes

excess.fromFood: No upper limit has been set, because the healthy kidney excretes a surplus readily — up to roughly 0.8–1.0 L per hour.
fromSupplements: frequent urination and disturbed sleep
dilutional hyponatraemia when intake exceeds renal clearance
excess.severeRisk: Drinking far beyond renal clearance dilutes plasma sodium and can cause cerebral oedema, seizures and death. This is rare but real, and is documented in endurance events and in water-drinking contests. Sustained intake above roughly 1 L/hour is where the risk begins.

absorption.typicalRate: Essentially complete, mostly in the small intestine
enhancers: small amounts of sodium and glucose, which drive co-transport
drinking steadily rather than in large single volumes
high-water foods, which arrive with electrolytes and are absorbed steadily
inhibitors: very high osmolality drinks, which can draw water into the gut
alcohol, which suppresses vasopressin and increases urinary loss
large single volumes, much of which are simply excreted
absorption.notes: Roughly 20% of total water intake comes from food, which is why the AI figures look higher than the amount anyone drinks. Fruit and vegetables are 80–95% water. Caffeinated drinks count toward intake — the diuretic effect is modest and does not offset the fluid they carry, contrary to long-standing advice.

interactions.effect: Sodium is the principal determinant of extracellular fluid volume, and small amounts aid intestinal water absorption through co-transport. Rehydrating with plain water after heavy sweat loss can worsen hyponatraemia.
Potassium governs intracellular fluid volume, complementing sodium's role outside the cell.
Fibre draws water into the stool to soften and bulk it. Raising fibre without raising fluid makes constipation worse.

citations.label: NASEM — Dietary Reference Intakes for Water, Potassium, Sodium, Chloride, and Sulfate
Valtin — "Drink at least eight glasses of water a day." Really? (Am J Physiol 2002)
